data.heading: Why does your building cost so much to cool?
data.lede: Because glass is your facade's biggest energy leak — and most of what comes through it isn't light.
body: Of the solar energy hitting your windows, only about a third is the visible light your tenants actually want. Roughly half is infrared heat, and the rest is UV — both invisible, both working against you: heating the floor plate, fading the fit-out and driving your chillers harder every afternoon.
bullets: ≈53% infrared heat — the cooling load you pay for
≈30% visible light — the only part you want
≈17% UV & HEV — fades interiors, affects occupant health

media.alt: Clean diagram: sun → glass facade cross-section with three labelled arrows (infrared 53%, visible light 30%, UV 17%) entering the building.

data.footnote: Source basis: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory — windows are the largest contributor to unwanted indoor heat gain.

data.heading: What is window film, actually?
data.lede: A precision optical filter for your facade — not a roll of dark plastic.
body: High-performance window film is engineered, layer by microscopic layer, to sort sunlight: reflect the infrared heat, block the UV, and let the visible light through. The measurement that matters is not how dark a film looks — it's how much total solar energy it rejects.
That's why the industry-standard numbers on this page are worth learning once: you'll be able to evaluate any film, from any brand, in about thirty seconds.
bullets: VLT — Visible Light Transmission: how much daylight comes through
IRR — Infrared Rejection: how much heat radiation is stopped
TSER — Total Solar Energy Rejected: the number that predicts your bill
UV+420™ — IrisPro's patented cut-off: beyond UV400, into HEV blue light

data.heading: Three beliefs that cost building owners money
data.lede: If a film supplier has told you any of these, you already know more than they think you do.

pairs.myth: Window film will make our office dark and gloomy.
pairs.fact: Spectrally-selective films reject up to 85% of solar heat while keeping up to 70% of visible light.
pairs.explanation: Heat lives mostly in the invisible infrared band — a film can target it precisely without darkening the room. Darkness is a design choice, not a requirement.

pairs.myth: The darker the film, the cooler the building.
pairs.fact: Heat rejection is measured by TSER, not by tint darkness — a light film can outperform a dark one.
pairs.explanation: A dyed dark film absorbs light but can still pass infrared heat. Always compare TSER and IRR numbers, never shade.

pairs.myth: Film is an expense — re-glazing is the real upgrade.
pairs.fact: Film delivers a comparable thermal upgrade at a fraction of re-glazing cost, with payback typically measured in a few years.
pairs.explanation: Illustrative example pending verified project data: a 10,000m² office saving ~28% cooling energy can recover the installation cost in roughly 2–3 years — with no facade downtime.

data.heading: Before you decide — the questions every building owner asks

items.question: Will window film make our interior noticeably darker?
items.answer: Not unless you want it to. Spectrally-selective films target invisible infrared heat, so you can keep up to 70% of visible light while rejecting most of the heat. Your consultant will show you samples on your actual glass before you commit.

items.question: How long does installation take, and do we need to close?
items.answer: Most commercial installations are done zone by zone, outside operating hours if needed — no facade works, no scaffolding for interior application, and each area is usable again the same day.

items.question: What is the realistic payback period?
items.answer: It depends on your glass area, orientation and tariff. As an illustrative example, buildings saving around 30% of cooling energy typically see payback in a few years — we'll calculate yours from your actual electricity bill during the free assessment. (Verified figures to be supplied.)

items.question: Does window film contribute to GBI or other green building certifications?
items.answer: Yes — high-performance film can contribute points under energy efficiency and indoor environmental quality categories. We provide the documentation your certification consultant needs.

items.question: What happens if the film fails or bubbles years later?
items.answer: Every installation is registered in the IrisPro eWarranty system with up to 10 years of performance warranty, honoured through our authorised dealer network — not a verbal promise.
